attributes.title: Level 1

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you create a new variable for both of your sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it important to use descriptive sprite names, instead of leaving it as “mySprite”?

❓ Why do you think the [stay in screen] block is important to a Player’s experience?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to notice that the order of the code blocks matters. Any block that refers to a sprite needs to come after its [set sprite to] block.
steps.instructions:
Code a Player and an Enemy sprite!


Set both sprite’s sprite kinds and positions. Set the Player sprite to move with direction buttons and stay in screen.


Be sure to name both sprites. This is also known as setting the sprite’s variable. You will learn about other variables in this level, too!


Click ▶ to see both sprites show up on screen.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite by updating the sprite names and adjusting the parameter?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens if the Enemy sprite’s speed is too high? What if it’s too low?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 While the Enemy sprite doesn’t have to be at the exact coordinates shown, it is important to have it reasonably far from the Player sprite. 

💡 Remind the ninjas that the goal is not to perfectly copy the example, but to find what works best for them.
steps.instructions:
Set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite.


Adjust the Enemy sprite’s speed by clicking the + in the [set sprite follow] block to edit the speed parameter. Try out different numbers until you find one that is challenging, but not impossible.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite follow the Player.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the [set life] block into the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How many lives should the Player sprite start with?

❓ Why is it helpful to have more than one life in a video game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja to try out different parameters. Just like with speed and other parameters, there is no perfect number of lives.
steps.instructions:
Add Player lives to the game.


Open the Info code block menu and drag a [set life to] block to the bottom of the [on start] container. The default parameter is 3; you can adjust the number to fit your game.


The [set life to] block adds another variable to the project. This variable will keep track of the Player’s lives, and update the number of lives each time 1 is lost.


Click ▶ to see the lives variable counter appear in the top left corner.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite kind in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Which sprite kind should you update—the first or second? What should you update it to?

❓ What number did you set the [change life by] parameter to? Did it work as you expected?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the Ninja to use Player as the first sprite kind in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container, then update the second otherSprite kind. This keeps the overlap events consistent in the code, helping to organize what happens when the Player sprite interacts with sprites of different kinds on screen.

💡 The sprite kind information will be used instead of the sprite names in the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. 

💡 This step will have unexpected effects. As the ninja is testing this step, they may notice that the life variable decreases immediately to 0. Encourage the ninja to move to the next step to see how to address this bug.
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite’s life to change by -1 when it overlaps with the Enemy sprite. 


Drag out an [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block, and change the second sprite kind to “Enemy”. Open the Info code block menu and drag a [change life by] block into the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container block. The lives parameter is set to -1 so that the variable decreases whenever the Player and Enemy sprites overlap.


Click ▶ to see how the lives variable works. Notice what happens when the Player and Enemy sprites overlap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the otherSprite bubble into the [set sprite position to] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Why does the [set sprite position] block fix this bug?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 When the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, the life value will change by -1. If the Player sprite continues to overlap the Enemy sprite, the life value will continue to decrease until it hits 0. By resetting the position of the Enemy sprite, it stops the interaction from happening and causes the life value to change only by -1.

💡 Remind the ninja that unexpected behavior and debugging is an essential part of coding. 

💡 The ninja can also try to duplicate the Enemy sprite’s original [set sprite position] block by right clicking, and selecting “Duplicate”. This will create a copy of that block with all the same parameters. Guide the ninja to drag the duplicated block to the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container.
steps.instructions:
Oh no, there is a bug! The game ends as soon as the Enemy sprite overlaps with the Player sprite. Since the [change life by] block is inside of the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container, the Player will continue to lose lives as long as the two sprites are overlapping. 


Debug this by separating the two sprites as soon as the Player loses one life.


Add a [set sprite position] block to the [on sprite overlaps sprite] container. Drag the red (otherSprite) bubble from the [on sprite overlaps sprite] block into the [set sprite position] block to replace the mySprite variable. Change the x and y values so that the Enemy sprite returns to its starting position after the two sprites overlap.


Click ▶ to see the Enemy sprite reset its position after it overlaps with the Player sprite.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the [start countdown] block to the [on start] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the countdown runs out?

❓Did you set the parameter in the [start countdown] block?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Share that the countdown’s Game Over effect is a default behavior, much like the [follow sprite] block’s speed of 100. This can be changed using other blocks.

💡 Guide ninjas to try out different amounts of time to make the game more interesting.
steps.instructions:
Add a timer to the game!


Open the Info code block menu, then drag the [start countdown] block into the bottom of the [on start] container block. Set the parameter to the number of seconds you want the game to last.


The [start countdown] block adds another variable to the project. This variable will keep track of the time once the game starts, and end when the timer reaches 0.


Click ▶ to see the timer count down as you play this game!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add the [use effect] block to the top of the [on countdown end] container, before the [game over] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution: 

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens now when the countdown ends? Why do you think that happened?

❓ Where should you place the [use effect] block so it changes the [game over] effect?

❓ What are other ways you could celebrate the Player’s victory?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Ask the ninja to think through different ways the game could end when the timer runs out.

💡Guide ninjas to place the [use effect] block above the [game over] block so it changes the effect before the game over code runs. This is similar to changing the dialog frame before using a [show long text] block.

💡 Let the ninja know that they can also add other sounds or effects inside the [on countdown end] container block to make the win more exciting.
steps.instructions:
The Player loses when time runs out, even if they still have lives! Since the goal is to avoid the Enemy, the Player sprite should win when time runs out.


Open the Info code block menu and drag out an [on countdown end] container block. Add a [game over] block into the [on countdown end] container, and leave the toggle set to WIN. 


Open the Game code block menu and drag the [use effect] block into the top of the [on countdown end] container, then choose a fun effect to play when the game ends.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the countdown ends!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you drag the background and splash screen code blocks inside the correct container block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

﻿

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions will help people understand how your project works?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project with a background color and add game instructions with a splash screen.


Click ▶ to see the completed game project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a game where the Player sprite must keep away from an Enemy sprite to not lose lives. Win by staying away from the Enemy sprite until the timer runs out.

validationItems.text: Set the 2 sprites’ names, sprite kinds, and positions.
Set the Enemy sprite to follow the Player sprite
Change the life variable when the Player sprite overlaps an Enemy sprite, then reset the Enemy sprite’s position.
When the countdown timer reaches 0, end the game in a win with a matching effect.
Add a background or splash screen with game directions.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Yellow Belt! In this level, you’ll learn about variables, which are pieces of data that can be stored, updated, and used in your programs. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Data Entry
badges.description: Use variables to keep track of data in a project.

badges.title: YOLO
badges.description: Set and change the lives variable in a project.

badges.title: Time Flies
badges.description: Set a countdown timer in a project.

badges.title: Keeping Track
badges.description: Set and change the score variable in a project.

badges.title: -poof-
badges.description: Destroy a sprite when something happens in a project.
